d: Ignorance; specifically: willful ignorance.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: Ignorance means a lack of knowledge or understanding. This word describes what a person does not know, rather than naming a specific action or emotion. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in 1 Corinthians 15:34 and 1 Peter 2:15. Its basic sense remains focused on unawareness or lack of understanding; the surrounding verse determines what particular knowledge is absent in each passage.

d: To put on, clothe.
me: Verb, peRfect, Passive, Participle, Accusative, Singular, Masculine
Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word refers to clothes or to the act of clothing and dressing someone. It can describe being dressed in garments or putting garments on another person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, appearing in passages that use clothing as an ordinary picture of outward appearance. Its basic meaning remains focused on garments and the act of covering a person with them; the surrounding verse determines whether it is best rendered “clothes,” “to clothe,” or “to dress.”

d: Renewing; a renewal or change of heart and life.
me: Noun, Dative, Singular, Feminine
Noun, Genitive, Singular, Feminine

e.t: Renewal means the process of becoming new again or being restored to a fresh condition. It describes a real change from an earlier state, with emphasis on restored newness rather than mere continuation. This Greek New Testament word occurs twice, in Romans 12:2 and Titus 3:5. In both places, its exact force depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains renewal: a change that brings fresh life or condition.

d: Antichrist, either one who puts himself in the place of, or the enemy (opponent) of the Messiah.

e.t: This word means “antichrist” and can also refer to more than one as “antichrists.” It is a title or designation used in the Greek New Testament for an opposing figure or figures identified by that name. The word appears five times in four verses, all in 1 John and 2 John. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the designation “antichrist.”

d: To push (thrust) away, repulse, reject, refuse.
me: Verb, Aorist, middle Deponent, Indicative, third, Plural
Verb, Aorist, middle Deponent, Indicative, third, Singular
Verb, Aorist, middle Deponent, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine
Verb, Present, middle or passive depoNent, Indicative, second, Plural

e.t: This word means “to reject” or “to refuse”—to push someone or something away rather than accept it. It can describe a deliberate decision not to receive, acknowledge, or continue with what is presented. In the Greek New Testament, it appears six times, including uses rendered “rejected” and “reject.” Its exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains active refusal or dismissal.

d: Now, just now, at this moment.
me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “now”. It points to the present time—the moment being spoken about, or the current stage of events. In the Greek New Testament, it appears 36 times across 35 verses, showing a recurring way to mark what is true or happening at the present point rather than at some distant time. Its basic force remains simple: it brings attention to the present. The surrounding verse determines whether “now” marks a present action, condition, or moment of transition.

e.t: This word means to forgive or release someone from a claim, debt, offense, or obligation. It can describe pardon—letting a person go free from what is held against them—or the act of releasing something or someone. The New Testament uses it broadly, appearing 143 times across 131 verses, so its precise emphasis depends on the surrounding sentence. Its central idea remains the removal of a restraint, debt, or charge rather than continuing to hold it.

d: To come to the rescue of, come to help, help.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, iMperative, second, Singular
Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, first, Singular
Verb, Aorist, Active, iNfinitive
Verb, Present, Active, iMperative, second, Plural
Verb, Present, Active, iMperative, second, Singular

e.t: This word means “to help”—to give aid, support, or assistance to someone in need. It expresses the action of coming to another’s aid rather than merely noticing a problem. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times, showing a recurring expression for practical or requested assistance. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central meaning remains the giving of help.

d: Gamaliel, a noted Pharisee, teacher of Saul.
me: Noun, Genitive, Singular, Masculine, Person
Noun, Nominative, Singular, Masculine, Person

e.t: Gamaliel is a personal name, referring to a man named Gamaliel rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, the name appears twice, both times in Acts: Acts 5:34 and Acts 22:3. The available wording identifies the name itself, while the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain what Gamaliel does or says in either passage.

d: To hold up as an example, make a show of, expose.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular
Verb, Aorist, Active, iNfinitive

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to disgrace” or “to expose to public disgrace.” It describes an action that puts a person openly into shame, making dishonor visible rather than keeping it private. The word appears twice in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew and Colossians, so its central idea is clear even though each passage must be read in its own setting. It focuses on public exposure and the resulting loss of honor, not merely on inward embarrassment.

d: Two thousand.
me: Adjective, Nominative, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word means “two thousand,” expressing a quantity of 2,000. It functions as a number word, identifying how many persons, things, or beings are being counted in a sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 5:13. Its meaning is precise and numerical rather than symbolic by itself; the surrounding passage determines what is being counted and how the number contributes to the statement.

d: Visible form, shape, appearance, outward show, kind, species, class.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Neuter
Noun, Dative, Singular, Neuter
Noun, Genitive, Singular, Neuter
Noun, Nominative, Singular, Neuter

e.t: This word means the visible form or appearance of something. It refers to how a person or thing is seen or presented outwardly, rather than describing an invisible idea alone. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, including uses rendered “form” and “appearance.” Its precise force in a particular sentence depends on what is being seen and the surrounding context, but its central sense remains the observable shape, look, or manifestation of something.

d: Willing, willingly, voluntarily.
me: Adjective, Nominative, Singular, Feminine
Adjective, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means “voluntarily”—doing something by one’s own choice rather than under compulsion. It describes willing action or acceptance and helps show that the person involved acts freely. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, so its meaning is focused and consistent rather than broad or varied across many passages. The surrounding verse determines what action is being done willingly, but the word itself emphasizes the absence of coercion.

d: Enoch, son of Jared and father of Methuselah.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Feminine
Noun, Genitive, Singular, Masculine, Person
Noun, Nominative, Singular, Masculine, Person

e.t: Enoch is a personal name, referring to a man identified by that name. In the Greek New Testament, it is rendered consistently as “Enoch,” rather than describing an object, action, or quality. The name appears three times, in Luke, Hebrews, and Jude. Its meaning here is therefore primarily identifying: it distinguishes Enoch as a particular person mentioned in the biblical record. The surrounding verse determines what is being said about him in each passage.

d: Since, forasmuch as.
me: CONJunction or conjunctive particle

e.t: This word means “inasmuch as” or “since,” introducing a reason or circumstance that provides the basis for what follows. It functions as a connecting word rather than naming a person, object, action, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 1:1. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its normal meaning points to something already true or recognized as the reason for the statement that follows.

d: To take to wife after, marry a deceased brother's wife.
me: Verb, Future, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to marry,” describing the act of entering marriage. It is a verb that refers specifically to marrying rather than to marriage as a general institution or relationship. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 22:24. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the action of marrying. The English rendering “marry” directly reflects this central sense.

d: To hunt, seek to catch or entrap; to lay hold of.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, iNfinitive

e.t: This word means “to catch,” including catching someone in a mistake or pursuing and catching something like prey. It describes the act of securing or trapping someone or something rather than merely noticing it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 11:54, so its broader range is established by its lexical meanings rather than by many passages. The surrounding verse determines exactly how the catching or trapping is being expressed there.

d: Jericho, a city a little north of the Dead Sea.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Feminine, Location
Noun, Genitive, Singular, Feminine, Location

e.t: This word is the name “Jericho,” referring to the place called Jericho in the Greek New Testament. It functions as a proper name rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. The name occurs seven times across six New Testament verses, appearing in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and Hebrews. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

d: A curse, an accursed thing.

e.t: This word means “curse” or “cursed thing.” As a noun, it can name the curse itself or something regarded as cursed. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Revelation 22:3. Its basic sense identifies what is under a curse or associated with a curse, while the surrounding passage determines the precise force of the term in that occurrence.

d: A downcast countenance as a sign of sorrow, gloominess, gloom, dejection.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: Gloominess means a dark, downcast state of mind or appearance. It is a noun describing the presence of gloom rather than an action someone performs. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, in James 4:9. The verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, so its precise force in that sentence must be understood from its context.

d: A couch, bed, portable bed or mat, a couch for reclining at meals, possibly also a bier.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Feminine
Noun, Genitive, Plural, Feminine
Noun, Genitive, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word means “bed,” referring to a place where someone lies or rests. It is an ordinary noun for a sleeping place or resting couch, and its use in the Greek New Testament covers nine occurrences. The word appears in passages involving people lying on beds, carrying a bed, or putting something on a bed. Its basic meaning remains physical and concrete; the surrounding verse determines the particular action or situation connected with the bed.

d: Reasoning, thinking; a conception, device.
me: Noun, Accusative, Plural, Masculine
Noun, Genitive, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This word means “thought” or “thoughts,” referring to what a person considers or holds in the mind. It describes inner thinking rather than an outward action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, showing a focused use for a person’s mental considerations. The exact force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains the thoughts formed within the mind.

d: The breast, pap.
me: Noun, Nominative, Plural, Masculine
Noun, Nominative, Singular, Neuter

e.t: This word refers to a breast, the part of the body associated with nursing and the nourishment of infants. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times: twice in Luke and once in Revelation. Its basic meaning remains a straightforward bodily reference, while the exact significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage. The word is used for both ordinary human anatomy and a bodily description in a vision.

d: A measure, whether lineal or cubic; a measuring rod.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Neuter
Noun, Dative, Singular, Neuter
Noun, Genitive, Singular, Neuter

e.t: This word means “measure”: an amount, standard, or means by which something is assessed or given. In the New Testament, it can describe a measured portion, a standard applied to others, or a degree allotted to a person. Its central idea is something fixed or proportioned rather than unlimited or undefined. The word occurs 14 times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in teaching about judgment, giving, spiritual assignment, and the dimensions of the heavenly city. Its precise force in any verse comes from the surrounding sentence and passage.

d: To commit adultery (of a man with a married woman, but also of a married man).
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, third, Singular
Verb, Present, Active, iNfinitive
Verb, Present, Passive, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word means “to commit adultery,” referring to sexual unfaithfulness in marriage. It functions as an action word, describing the act rather than merely an attitude or desire. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 15 times across 12 verses, including teachings about God’s command against adultery and statements concerning marriage and divorce. Its central meaning remains consistent wherever it appears: violating the marriage relationship through adultery. The surrounding verse determines how the action is applied in each passage.

d: Form, shape, outward appearance.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Feminine
Noun, Dative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word means “form,” referring to the outward or recognizable form of someone or something. It can identify what a person is seen to be, while also pointing to the nature or condition expressed in that form. In the New Testament, it occurs three times: once in Mark and twice in Philippians. Its basic meaning remains “form”; the surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is on appearance, status, or the condition being expressed. The word is translated consistently as “form.”

d: Autumn, autumnal fruits.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “fruit,” referring to produce that comes from a plant or tree. As a noun, it names the tangible result yielded by growing things. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Revelation 18:14. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains straightforward: fruit or agricultural produce. This is a distinct Greek New Testament word and should be understood within that corpus rather than treated as a Hebrew or Greek LXX entity.

d: A deposit, anything committed to one's charge or trust.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word means “deposit”: something entrusted to another person for safekeeping or faithful care. It points to a valuable trust that must be guarded and preserved rather than neglected or abandoned. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in 1 and 2 Timothy, where its basic sense concerns something placed in someone’s care. The surrounding passage determines what the deposit specifically is in each occurrence.

gl: to be out of one's mind
d: To be out of my senses, to be beside myself.
me: Verb, Present, Active, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “be insane” or “to be out of one's mind.” It describes a person whose thinking or behavior is regarded as irrational, beyond sound judgment. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 11:23. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense is a strong description of mental or behavioral irrationality, not merely ordinary confusion or a small mistake.

e.t: This word means “to test” or “to tempt”: it describes putting someone or something to the test, sometimes with the aim of exposing what is true and sometimes by trying to lead someone into wrongdoing. Its meaning therefore depends on whether the testing is presented as a trial or as enticement. The word appears 38 times in the Greek New Testament, including uses describing Jesus being tempted and people testing Him. Its central idea is putting someone to a proving test.

d: A striker, contentious person, brawler.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word describes a bully or violent man—a person characterized by forceful or intimidating behavior. It refers to a person’s character, not merely to one isolated violent act. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice: once in 1 Timothy 3:3 and once in Titus 1:7. The surrounding wording in each passage determines how this description functions there, but its central sense remains a person marked by bullying or violence.

d: A voyage, sailing.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Masculine
Noun, Genitive, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means “voyage,” referring to travel by sea from one place to another. It names the journey itself rather than the ship, sailor, or destination. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Acts, where it concerns travel by sea. The word therefore has a clear, practical sense: a planned or ongoing voyage, especially one involving a journey across the water. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

gl: to commit sexual immorality of any kind
d: To fornicate; to practice idolatry.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Plural
Verb, peRfect, Active, Participle, Nominative, Plural, Masculine
Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, third, Singular
Verb, Present, Active, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Masculine
Verb, Present, Active, Subjunctive, first, Plural

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to commit sexual immorality of any kind” or “to sin sexually.” It describes the act of engaging in sexual wrongdoing, rather than merely referring to a person or condition. The word occurs eight times in seven New Testament verses, especially in 1 Corinthians and Revelation. Its use includes direct warnings about sexual sin and descriptions of people or communities involved in it. The surrounding passage determines the particular situation, but the word itself consistently points to committing sexual immorality.

d: To be red, fire-colored.
me: Verb, Present, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “be (fiery) red” or “to be red.” It describes something showing a red color, with the gloss suggesting a vivid or fiery shade rather than merely naming redness as an abstract idea. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Matthew 16:2–3. Its normal meaning is straightforward, while the surrounding verse determines what is being described as red in each occurrence.

d: A basket, generally of twisted cords.
me: Noun, Dative, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “basket,” referring to a container used to carry or hold things. It names an ordinary physical object rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at 2 Corinthians 11:33, so its meaning is narrowly established by that single use and the direct gloss “basket.” The surrounding verse supplies the particular situation in which the basket appears.

d: A Scythian, as typical of the uncivilized.
me: Noun, Nominative, Singular, Masculine, Location Gentilic

e.t: This word means “Scythian,” referring to a person identified as belonging to the Scythians. It functions as a people-group designation rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual condition. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Colossians 3:11. The word itself identifies a person by people-group identity; the surrounding verse determines how that designation functions in its particular statement. Its direct meaning remains the same: a Scythian person.

d: (a) a general or leader of the army, (b) a magistrate or governor, (c) captain of the temple.
me: Noun, Accusative, Plural, Masculine
Noun, Dative, Plural, Masculine
Noun, Nominative, Plural, Masculine
Noun, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This Greek New Testament word refers to a commander, magistrate, or officer—someone holding recognized authority. It is a title for a public official rather than a general description of any person in charge. The word occurs 10 times in the Greek New Testament, appearing twice in Luke and eight times in Acts. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on the surrounding context, but its central sense is an official exercising authority.

d: To thrust down to Tartarus or Gehenna.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to condemn” or “to send to hell.” It expresses a decisive judgment that assigns someone to punishment, rather than merely criticizing or warning them. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in 2 Peter 2:4. Its exact force in that verse is understood from the surrounding passage, but its central meaning concerns condemnation and consignment to hell.

d: Fortunatus, a Christian of Corinth.
me: Noun, Genitive, Singular, Masculine, Person

e.t: Fortunatus is a personal name, referring to a man named in the Greek New Testament. The name appears once, in 1 Corinthians 16:17, and is rendered “Fortunatus.” Because it is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object, its basic meaning is the identification of this individual. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain his specific role or significance in that passage.

d: A palisade, mound for besieging.
me: Noun, Accusative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means "barricade": an obstruction set up to block or restrict movement. It names a concrete blocking barrier rather than an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 19:43. The surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain how the term functions in that particular scene; the word itself supplies the idea of a barrier that prevents or limits passage.

d: Omega, the last letter of the Greek alphabet.
me: Noun, Genitive, Singular, Feminine

e.t: This word refers to the Greek alphabet letter called “Omega.” It is a name for that letter rather than a description of an action, person, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in Revelation: Revelation 1:8, 21:6, and 22:13. Its precise significance in each passage depends on the verse wording and surrounding context, which are not included here. The word itself identifies Omega as an alphabetic letter.

me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Participle, Genitive, Plural, Masculine

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to kindle,” describing the act of setting something alight or causing it to burn. It expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Luke 22:55. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of kindling or lighting a fire.
